```text
1	# Student Guide — Running Gitea Locally
2	
3	Welcome! This is a course fork of [Gitea](https://about.gitea.com/), a self-hosted Git service
4	written in **Go** (backend) and **Vue/TypeScript** (frontend). You'll be improving the kind of tool
5	you use every day — issues, pull requests, code review, CI/Actions.
6	
7	This guide gets you from a fresh clone to a running Gitea on your machine, backed by **SQLite** (no
8	separate database server needed). It should take ~15–30 minutes, most of which is the first backend
9	compile.
10	
11	---
12	
13	## 1. Prerequisites
14	
15	Install these before you start. Versions below are the minimums this fork is pinned to.
16	
17	| Tool | Version | Notes |
18	| --- | --- | --- |
19	| **Go** | **1.26.4+** | Backend. `go.mod` requires `go 1.26.4`. |
20	| **Node.js** | **22.18.0+** | Frontend build only (not needed at runtime). |
21	| **pnpm** | **11.0.0+** | Frontend package manager. Easiest via `corepack enable`. |
22	| **Git** | 2.x | Required both to build **and at runtime** (Gitea shells out to git). |
23	
24	> 💡 **New to Go?** Gitea's backend is written in Go. [A Tour of Go](https://go.dev/tour/) is the official interactive tutorial (~2 hours) and covers everything you need for typical backend tasks. Pay attention to goroutines and interfaces — both appear frequently in this codebase.
25	
26	> 📖 **Developer docs:** [`docs/development.md`](docs/development.md) in this repo covers the development workflow, how to run tests, database migration conventions, and the overall package structure. Read it before picking a task.
27	
28	**You do NOT need a C compiler (gcc).** This version of Gitea uses a pure-Go SQLite driver
29	(`modernc.org/sqlite`) and builds with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, so there's no MSYS2/MinGW/Xcode-tools step.
30	This is the main reason setup is painless on Windows.
31	
32	**Optional:** `make` (convenience only — every command below also has a no-`make` form), and Docker
33	(if you'd rather run the official container instead of building).
34	
35	### Installing the toolchain
36	- **Windows:** `winget install GoLang.Go` and `winget install OpenJS.NodeJS`, then `corepack enable`.
37	- **macOS:** `brew install go node` then `corepack enable`.
38	- **Linux:** use your package manager (or the official Go tarball) for Go + Node, then `corepack enable`.
39	
40	Verify:
41	```bash
42	go version      # go1.26.x
43	node --version  # v22.18+ (or newer)
44	pnpm --version  # 11.x
45	git --version
46	```
47	
48	---
49	
50	## 2. Get the code
51	
52	```bash
53	git clone https://github.com/musta55/gitea.git
54	cd gitea
55	```
56	
57	---
58	
59	## 3. Build
60	
61	Gitea is built in two halves: the frontend assets (with pnpm/vite) and the backend binary (with Go).
62	
63	### Option A — with `make` (recommended if you have it)
64	```bash
65	make build          # builds frontend + backend into ./gitea (or gitea.exe on Windows)
66	```
67	
68	### Option B — without `make` (works everywhere)
69	```bash
70	# 1) frontend assets -> public/assets/
71	pnpm install
72	pnpm exec vite build
73	
74	# 2) backend binary  (pure-Go SQLite, no gcc)
75	#    Linux/macOS:
76	CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o gitea .
77	#    Windows (PowerShell):
78	$env:CGO_ENABLED=0; go build -buildmode=exe -o gitea.exe .
79	```
80	
81	> The first backend compile takes a few minutes and produces a ~100+ MB binary. Later builds are fast.
82	
83	---
84	
85	## 4. Run (SQLite, zero config)
86	
87	Just start the web server from the repo root and let the built-in installer set everything up:
88	
89	```bash
90	# Linux/macOS:
91	./gitea web
92	# Windows:
93	./gitea.exe web
94	```
95	
96	Then open **http://localhost:3000** and you'll see the **Install** page:
97	
98	1. **Database Type:** choose **SQLite3** (the default path is fine).
99	2. Leave the rest at defaults for local dev.
100	3. Expand **Administrator Account Settings** and create your admin username / password / email
101	   (do this now so you don't have to register separately).
102	4. Click **Install Gitea**.
103	
104	That's it — you now have a running Gitea with a SQLite database at `data/gitea.db`. Log in with the
105	admin account you just created.
106	
107	> **Port already in use?** If something else owns `:3000`, start Gitea on another port:
108	> `./gitea web --port 3030` and open http://localhost:3030 instead.
109	
110	### On macOS
111	The same `./gitea web` command works — a few Mac-specific notes:
112	
113	- **Firewall prompt:** the first launch may ask *"Do you want the application `gitea` to accept
114	  incoming network connections?"* — click **Allow** (it's the binary you just built).
115	- **`permission denied`:** make the binary executable first: `chmod +x gitea`.
116	- **Gatekeeper "cannot be opened" warning:** only affects binaries downloaded from a browser, not
117	  ones you built yourself. If you ever run a downloaded release binary instead, clear the
118	  quarantine flag: `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ./gitea`.
119	- **Apple Silicon (M1–M4):** fully supported — Go produces a native arm64 binary, nothing extra to do.
120	
121	### Live-reload while developing (optional)
122	If you have `make`:
123	```bash
124	make watch          # rebuilds frontend + backend on file changes (uses air)
125	```
126	
127	---
128	
129	## 5. Try it out
130	
131	Create a repository (with "Initialize repository"), open an issue, push a branch, and open a pull
132	request so you can see the code-review UI. These are the areas most course tasks touch:
133	
134	- **Code review UI** — the diff viewer and PR review flow.
135	- **Issues / Kanban** — issue tracking and project boards.
136	- **CI / Actions** — the built-in Actions runner and workflow UI.
137	
138	---
139	
140	## 6. Running the tests
141	
142	Gitea's test suite is validated on **Linux CI**. Run it on Linux, macOS, WSL2, or the provided
143	`.devcontainer` — **not native Windows**, where a handful of unit tests fail for platform reasons
144	(symlink semantics, temp-file cleanup) rather than real bugs.
145	
146	```bash
147	# unit tests
148	CGO_ENABLED=0 go test ./...
149	# or, with make:
150	make test-backend         # unit tests
151	make test-integration     # integration tests (defaults to SQLite via GITEA_TEST_DATABASE)
152	```
153	
154	Frontend tests:
155	```bash
156	pnpm exec vitest run
157	```
158	
159	---
160	
161	## 7. Common gotchas
162	
163	- **`git` not found at runtime:** Gitea runs git commands for every repo operation. Make sure `git`
164	  is on your `PATH`, not just in your IDE.
165	- **`go build` is slow the first time:** normal — it compiles ~3000 packages once, then caches.
166	- **Don't commit build artifacts:** `gitea`/`gitea.exe`, `data/`, `custom/`, and `public/assets/*`
167	  are gitignored. Keep them out of your commits.
168	- **Windows line endings:** the repo expects LF. Your editor/`.gitattributes` should keep it that way.
169	
170	---
171	
172	---
173	
174	## Contributing workflow
175	
176	All team members have write access to this repository, so the team uses a **branch-based** workflow — not forks. Here is the background and the commands.
177	
178	**Why not forks?** Forking is the standard model for contributing to open-source projects where you _don't_ have write access: you fork to your own GitHub account, clone your fork, and open a PR from your fork back to the original. You will encounter this when contributing to the upstream project. But for your course team — where everyone has write access to the shared repo — it just adds confusion: two clones on your machine, two remotes to keep in sync, merge conflicts that are harder to reason about.
179	
180	**Branch-based workflow** is what most professional teams use internally. You clone the shared repo once, create a short-lived branch for each issue, push the branch back to the same repo, and open a PR from that branch into `main`. One clone, one remote, full PR workflow.
181	
182	### For each issue you work on
183	
184	```bash
185	# One-time setup: clone the team repo (skip if already done)
186	git clone https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea.git
187	cd gitea
188	
189	# Before starting each issue: make sure you are on a fresh main
190	git checkout main
191	git pull origin main
192	
193	# Create a branch named for the issue
194	git checkout -b feat/issue-17-dark-mode      # new feature
195	git checkout -b fix/issue-42-toast-dismiss   # bug fix
196	
197	# ... make your changes, run tests ...
198	
199	# Stage and commit
200	git add <the files you changed>
201	git commit -m "feat: add dark mode toggle (#17)"
202	
203	# Push the branch to the team repo
204	git push origin feat/issue-17-dark-mode
205	```
206	
207	After pushing, GitHub shows a **"Compare & pull request"** banner on the repository page. Click it to open a PR from your branch into `main`. Fill in the description (what changed and why), reference the issue (`Closes #17`), and request a review from a teammate.
208	
209	**Branch naming:**
210	
211	| Prefix | Use for |
212	|---|---|
213	| `feat/issue-<N>-short-description` | new features |
214	| `fix/issue-<N>-short-description` | bug fixes |
215	| `chore/short-description` | docs, config, dependency updates |
216	
217	> ⚠️ **`main` is protected — direct pushes are blocked.** All changes go through a reviewed PR. If you accidentally commit to `main` locally, move your changes to a branch before pushing:
218	>
219	> ```bash
220	> git checkout -b fix/issue-42-my-fix   # create branch from your current state
221	> git checkout main
222	> git reset --hard origin/main          # revert local main to match remote
223	> ```
224	
225	**After your PR is merged**, delete the branch to keep the repo tidy:
226	
227	```bash
228	git checkout main
229	git pull origin main
230	git branch -d feat/issue-17-dark-mode
231	```
232	
233	## 8. Project documentation & policies (required reading)
234	
235	📚 **Official documentation:** <https://docs.gitea.com/> — usage, administration, and development
236	guides.
237	
238	Gitea has its own established contribution processes. They are **not restated here** — you are
239	responsible for finding, reading, and following them from the sources below:
240	
241	| You must take care of | Where to find it |
242	| --- | --- |
243	| How to use the tool | <https://docs.gitea.com/> |
244	| Code review process | [CONTRIBUTING.md — Code review](CONTRIBUTING.md#code-review) |
245	| Bug / issue resolution process | [CONTRIBUTING.md — How to report issues](CONTRIBUTING.md#how-to-report-issues) |
246	| Pull request conventions & PR policies | [CONTRIBUTING.md — Pull request format](CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-request-format) + [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) (commit/PR conventions) |
247	| AI policies | [CONTRIBUTING.md — AI Contribution Policy](CONTRIBUTING.md#ai-contribution-policy) + [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) |
248
```
</details></tool-use>

```text
1	# Development
2	
3	This document describes how to build Gitea from source and the day-to-day
4	development workflow. For prerequisites and how to obtain the code, see
5	[build-setup.md](build-setup.md). For running tests, see [testing.md](testing.md). For the
6	contribution workflow and review process, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md).
7	
8	Area-specific guidelines:
9	
10	- [Backend development guidelines](guidelines-backend.md)
11	- [Frontend development guidelines](guidelines-frontend.md)
12	- [Refactoring guidelines](guidelines-refactoring.md)
13	
14	## Building
15	
16	To build Gitea for development, run:
17	
18	```bash
19	make build
20	```
21	
22	No build tags are required: SQLite support is compiled in by default, which is
23	enough for local development. The `build` target runs two sub-targets, `frontend`
24	and `backend`. The `bindata` tag embeds the frontend assets into the binary and is
25	only needed when packaging a self-contained build, so leave it out during
26	development.
27	
28	See `make help` for all available targets, and the workflows in
29	[`.github/workflows`](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/tree/main/.github/workflows)
30	to see how continuous integration builds and checks Gitea.
31	
32	## Building continuously
33	
34	To rebuild automatically when source files change:
35	
36	```bash
37	# watch both frontend and backend
38	make watch
39	
40	# or watch only the frontend (starts the Vite dev server)
41	make watch-frontend
42	
43	# or watch only the backend (Go)
44	make watch-backend
45	```
46	
47	Watching all backend source files may hit the default open-files limit on macOS or
48	Linux; raise it with `ulimit -n 12288` for the current shell, or in your shell
49	startup file to make it permanent.
50	
51	## Formatting, linting and checks
52	
53	Continuous integration rejects pull requests that fail formatting, linting, or
54	consistency checks. Format your code first:
55	
56	```bash
57	make fmt
58	```
59	
60	Then lint:
61	
62	```bash
63	# lint everything
64	make lint
65	# or only one side
66	make lint-backend
67	make lint-frontend
68	```
69	
70	Many linters can fix issues automatically with `make lint-fix` (or the scoped
71	`make lint-backend-fix` / `make lint-frontend-fix`). The combined consistency
72	checks that CI runs are available as `make checks`.
73	
74	## Building and adding SVGs
75	
76	SVG icons are built with `make svg`, which compiles the icon sources into
77	`public/assets/img/svg`. Custom icons can be added under `web_src/svg`.
78	
79	## Updating the API
80	
81	When you create or change API routes, you **must** update the
82	[Swagger](https://swagger.io/docs/specification/2-0/what-is-swagger/) documentation
83	using [go-swagger](https://goswagger.io/) comments. See the
84	[backend development guidelines](guidelines-backend.md) for how API routes,
85	request/response structs, and swagger definitions fit together.
86	
87	Regenerate and validate the spec after changing an endpoint, then commit the
88	updated JSON:
89	
90	```bash
91	make generate-swagger
92	make swagger-validate
93	```
94	
95	CI verifies the committed spec is up to date with:
96	
97	```bash
98	make swagger-check
99	```
100	
101	## Creating new configuration options
102	
103	When adding configuration options it is not enough to add them to the
104	`modules/setting` files. Also update
105	[`custom/conf/app.example.ini`](../custom/conf/app.example.ini), and document them in
106	the [configuration cheat sheet](https://docs.gitea.com/administration/config-cheat-sheet),
107	which lives in the [documentation repository](https://gitea.com/gitea/docs).
108	
109	## Database migrations
110	
111	If you make breaking changes to a database-persisted struct under `models/`, add a
112	new migration in `models/migrations/`. See [testing.md](testing.md#migration-tests)
113	for running the migration tests.
114	
115	## Testing
116	
117	For unit, integration, end-to-end, and migration tests, see [testing.md](testing.md).
118	
119	## IDE configuration
120	
121	### Visual Studio Code
122	
123	A `launch.json` and `tasks.json` are provided in
124	[`contrib/development/vscode`](../contrib/development/vscode). See
125	[`contrib/development/README.md`](../contrib/development/README.md) for details.
126	
127	### GoLand
128	
129	Clicking the `Run Application` arrow on `func main()` in `/main.go` starts a
130	debuggable Gitea instance.
131	
132	The `Output Directory` in `Run/Debug Configuration` **must** be set to the Gitea
133	project directory (the one containing `main.go` and `go.mod`). Otherwise the working
134	directory is a GoLand temporary directory, which prevents Gitea from loading dynamic
135	resources (such as templates) in development.
136	
137	## Submitting your changes
138	
139	Push your branch and open a pull request. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md)
140	for the review process and PR requirements. For help, join the `#Develop` channel on
141	[Discord](https://discord.gg/gitea).
142
```
</details></tool-use>

```text
1	# Backend development guidelines
2	
3	This document covers backend-specific architecture and contribution expectations.
4	For the general workflow see [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md), and for building
5	and testing see [development.md](development.md) and [testing.md](testing.md).
6	
7	## Background
8	
9	The backend is written in Go. Web routing is handled by
10	[chi](https://github.com/go-chi/chi) and database access goes through the
11	[XORM](https://xorm.io/) ORM. Understanding how the packages depend on each other is
12	essential before contributing backend code.
13	
14	## Package design
15	
16	### Package layout
17	
18	The backend is split into top-level packages, each with a focused responsibility:
19	
20	- `build`: helper scripts used at compile time
21	- `cmd`: subcommands such as `web`, `serv`, `hooks`, `doctor`, and admin utilities
22	- `models`: data structures and database operations (XORM); keeps external
23	  dependencies to a minimum
24	  - `models/db`: core database operations
25	  - `models/fixtures`: sample data used by tests
26	  - `models/migrations`: schema migration scripts
27	- `modules`: standalone functionality with few dependencies
28	  - `modules/setting`: configuration handling
29	  - `modules/git`: interaction with the Git command line
30	- `routers`: request handlers, split into `api`, `web`, `install`, and `private`
31	- `services`: business logic that ties routers and models together
32	- `templates`: Go HTML templates
33	- `public`: compiled frontend assets
34	- `tests`: integration and end-to-end test helpers
35	
36	### Dependency direction
37	
38	Dependencies only flow in one direction:
39	
40	```text
41	cmd → routers → services → models → modules
42	```
43	
44	A package on the left may import a package on its right, but never the reverse.
45	
46	### Naming conventions
47	
48	- Top-level packages use the plural form: `services`, `models`, `routers`.
49	- Subpackages use the singular form: `services/user`, `models/repository`.
50	
51	When packages from different layers share a name, use a snake_case import alias to
52	disambiguate:
53	
54	```go
55	import user_service "gitea.dev/services/user"
56	```
57	
58	### Database transactions
59	
60	Operations that must roll back together should run inside `db.WithTx()` (or
61	`db.WithTx2()` when a value must be returned), defined in `models/db/context.go`.
62	Functions that participate in a transaction take a `context.Context` as their first
63	parameter so the transaction can be propagated.
64	
65	### XORM gotchas
66	
67	- Never call `x.Update(exemplar)` without an explicit `WHERE` clause — it updates
68	  every row in the table.
69	- Partial table migrations must use `SyncWithOptions(IgnoreDrop...)` rather than a
70	  plain `Sync`.
71	- When inserting rows with preset IDs, MSSQL requires `SET IDENTITY_INSERT` to be
72	  enabled and PostgreSQL requires the sequence to be updated afterwards.
73	
74	## Dependencies
75	
76	Go dependencies are managed with [Go Modules](https://go.dev/ref/mod).
77	
78	Pull requests should only modify `go.mod` and `go.sum` where it relates to the
79	change at hand, be it a bug fix or a new feature. Otherwise, these files should only
80	be touched by pull requests whose sole purpose is updating dependencies. Run
81	`make tidy` after any change to `go.mod`.
82	
83	Any `go.mod` / `go.sum` update must be justified in the PR description and must be
84	verified by reviewers and the merger to reference an existing upstream commit.
85	
86	## API v1
87	
88	The API is documented with [Swagger](https://gitea.com/api/swagger) and is modelled
89	on [the GitHub API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest).
90	
91	### GitHub API compatibility
92	
93	Gitea's API should use the same endpoints and fields as the GitHub API where
94	possible, unless there is a good reason to deviate.
95	
96	- If Gitea offers functionality GitHub does not, a new endpoint may be added.
97	- If Gitea exposes information the GitHub API does not, a new field may be added as
98	  long as it does not collide with a GitHub field.
99	- Existing fields should not be removed unless there is a strong reason; the same
100	  applies to status responses.
101	
102	If you notice a problem that would require a breaking change, leave a comment in the
103	code for a future refactor to API v2 (which is currently not planned) rather than
104	breaking v1.
105	
106	### Adding and maintaining API routes
107	
108	- All possible results (errors, success, and failure messages) must be documented in
109	  the swagger comments on the route.
110	- Every JSON request body must be defined as a struct in `modules/structs/` and
111	  registered in [`routers/api/v1/swagger/options.go`](../routers/api/v1/swagger/options.go).
112	- Every JSON response must be defined as a struct in `modules/structs/` and
113	  registered with its category under [`routers/api/v1/swagger/`](../routers/api/v1/swagger).
114	
115	### HTTP methods and status codes
116	
117	In general, choose HTTP methods as follows:
118	
119	- **GET** returns the requested object(s) with status **200 OK**.
120	- **POST** creates a new object (e.g. a user) and returns **201 Created** with the
121	  created object.
122	- **PUT** adds or assigns an existing object (e.g. a user to a team) and returns
123	  **204 No Content** with no body.
124	- **PATCH** edits an existing object and returns the changed object with **200 OK**.
125	- **DELETE** removes an object and returns **204 No Content** with no body.
126	
127	### Requirements for API routes
128	
129	- All parameters of endpoints that edit an object must be optional, except those
130	  needed to identify the object, which are required.
131	- Endpoints returning lists must support pagination (`page` and `limit` query
132	  options) and set the `X-Total-Count` header via `ctx.SetTotalCountHeader(...)`.
133
```

## Gitea Architecture Overview

Gitea is a self-hosted Git service: **Go** backend (chi router + XORM ORM) and **Vue/TypeScript** frontend (Vite build, Fomantic-UI + some Tailwind). It's a fairly large, layered codebase — the good news is the layering is strict and well-documented (`docs/guidelines-backend.md`), so once you know the rule, the rest is just "which layer does this file live in."

### The one rule that explains everything

Dependencies flow **one direction only**:

```
cmd → routers → services → models → modules
```

A package can import anything to its right, never to its left. So `modules/` code can't import `models/`, and `models/` can't import `services/`. This is why, e.g., git-shelling-out logic lives in `modules/git` (no DB knowledge needed) while "create a PR and notify watchers" lives in `services/pull` (needs both DB access *and* orchestration).

Naming convention: top-level packages are plural (`services`, `models`, `routers`), subpackages are singular (`services/user`, `models/repository`).

---

### Backend, layer by layer

**`cmd/`** — CLI subcommands: `web` (start the HTTP server), `serv`/`hooks` (invoked by git itself for SSH/push hooks), `admin`, `doctor`, `actions`, etc. This is the entry point layer — thin, just wires flags to the right router/service call.

**`routers/`** — HTTP request handlers only (parse request → call a service → render response). Split into:
- `routers/web` — the actual website (`repo`, `user`, `org`, `admin`, `explore`, `auth`...) — renders `templates/`
- `routers/api/v1` — the REST API (Swagger-documented, modeled on GitHub's API)
- `routers/api/actions`, `routers/api/packages` — Actions (CI) and package registry APIs
- `routers/install` — the first-run install wizard you'll see at `localhost:3000`
- `routers/private` — internal endpoints only the `serv`/`hooks` subcommands call, not public

**`services/`** — business logic; this is where routers and models get tied together. Look here for "what actually happens" on any action: `services/pull` (PR merge logic), `services/issue`, `services/mailer`, `services/webhook`, `services/actions` (CI runner orchestration), `services/auth` (login/OAuth2/2FA), `services/repository`, `services/markup` (rendering Markdown), etc.

**`models/`** — data structures + XORM database operations, kept dependency-light. `models/db` has the core transaction helpers (`db.WithTx()`), `models/migrations` has schema migrations (add one here whenever you change a persisted struct), `models/fixtures` has sample test data. Subpackages mirror the domain: `models/repo`, `models/issues`, `models/user`, `models/actions`, `models/perm` (permissions), etc.

**`modules/`** — standalone, low-dependency utility packages usable by any layer above. Notable ones: `modules/git` (shelling out to the git binary), `modules/setting` (config/`app.ini` parsing), `modules/structs` (API request/response JSON structs — every API type lives here), `modules/queue`, `modules/cache`, `modules/log`, `modules/markup`, `modules/ssh`, `modules/storage` (local/S3/etc. abstraction).

**Important pattern:** when a subpackage name collides across layers (e.g. `services/user` and `models/user`), imports get a snake_case alias like `user_service "gitea.dev/services/user"` — you'll see this constantly.

---

### Frontend

- **`web_src/js`** — TypeScript source: `components` (Vue SFCs), `features` (page-specific behavior wired up on load), `modules`, `webcomponents`, `markup` (rendering helpers for the diff/markdown views)
- **`web_src/css`** — styles (Fomantic-UI theme overrides + Tailwind utilities)
- **`templates/`** — server-rendered Go HTML templates (`repo`, `user`, `org`, `admin`, `mail`, `webhook`...) — these are what `routers/web` executes; Vue components get mounted into specific spots inside them
- **`public/`** — compiled output (`public/assets/`) — gitignored, produced by `pnpm exec vite build`
- **`web_src/svg`** — custom icon sources, compiled by `make svg`

---

### Tests

- `models/*/  *_test.go`, `modules/*_test.go` etc. — unit tests next to the code (`go test ./...`)
- `tests/integration` — full-stack tests against a real (SQLite by default) DB
- `tests/e2e` — Playwright browser tests
- `tests/fuzz` — fuzz targets
- `web_src/js/**/*.test.ts` — Vitest frontend unit tests

---

### Where to go deeper

- `docs/guidelines-backend.md` — the source for the layering/naming rules above, plus API conventions (HTTP verbs, pagination, swagger)
- `docs/guidelines-frontend.md` — Vue/TS conventions
- `docs/testing.md` — how each test tier runs

Given the course tasks mentioned in `STUDENTS.md` (code review UI, issues/Kanban, CI/Actions), you'd mostly be working in `routers/web/repo` + `services/pull`/`services/issue` + `templates/repo` + `web_src/js/components` for those features — that's a good place to start poking around rather than trying to read everything at once.

Want me to walk through one specific feature end-to-end (e.g. "what happens when you open a PR") to see how a request actually flows through these layers?

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-03 19:56:54Z)**_

Good question — this cuts right to a real software-engineering design principle, and the answer has two layers: a hard technical one (Go won't even let you) and a design one (why the rule exists on purpose, and how real needs for "backward" communication get satisfied without breaking it).

### First, the hard constraint

In Go, a direct cycle — package A imports B and B imports A — is a **compile error** (`import cycle not allowed`), not a style violation. So "models imports services, services imports models" literally cannot build. That's stronger than most languages (Java/Python/C++ will let you shoot yourself in the foot; Go's compiler refuses).

What *can* still happen, and is the real danger, is an **indirect** cycle: `models/repo` imports `modules/foo`, and `modules/foo` imports `models/user`, and `models/user` imports `models/repo` → cycle, three hops away, much harder to spot than a direct one. This is why the rule is stated as a whole-codebase policy (`cmd → routers → services → models → modules`) rather than "just don't write an obvious cycle" — it's a discipline that prevents the graph from tangling as ~3000 packages grow, not just a fix for the compiler error.

### If it were allowed anyway — what breaks

Say `modules/git` could import `services/pull` (to, e.g., trigger PR-merge logic directly when it detects a push). Consequences:

- **No blast radius.** Right now, if you touch `modules/git`, you know only `models`/`services`/`routers`/`cmd` code above it could be affected — never the reverse. Bidirectional deps mean a change anywhere can ripple anywhere, so "what might I break" stops being answerable by reading imports and becomes "run everything and see."
- **Testability collapses.** `modules/` is deliberately low-dependency so it can be unit-tested in isolation (spin up git, no DB, no HTTP). If it depended on `services`, testing `modules/git` would require standing up business logic, mailers, webhooks — the opposite of a unit test.
- **Reuse dies.** `modules/git` is usable by `serv`/`hooks` (called directly by git over SSH, no HTTP server running) precisely because it doesn't know `services` or `routers` exist. Wire it to `services/pull` and you can no longer use it standalone.
- **No map for newcomers.** Like you're doing right now — the whole reason I could describe the codebase by layer is that the layer *is* the map. Bidirectional deps turn the diagram into a hairball; you'd have to read call graphs, not directory names, to understand anything.
- **Slower builds.** Go compiles independent packages in parallel and caches per-package. A tangled graph means touching a "low" package forces recompiling everything that (indirectly) touches it both ways — cache invalidation spreads instead of staying contained.

This is the general **Acyclic Dependencies Principle** from software architecture — Gitea isn't inventing it, just applying it strictly.

### Are there legitimate cases that *want* two-way communication?

Yes — plenty. E.g., "when an issue is created (a `models`-level DB write), send an email, fire a webhook, index it for search, notify the Actions runner." That's four separate higher-layer concerns that all need to react to one low-level event. The naive way to do that would be for the model code to call each of those services directly — which would violate the direction rule.

Gitea's actual answer: **`services/notify`**. It defines a `Notifier` interface with methods like `IssueChangeStatus(...)`, and a `RegisterNotifier()` function. `services/mailer`, `services/webhook`, `services/actions`, and the indexer each implement that interface and register themselves at startup. Code that creates/changes an issue (still inside `services`, one layer, not crossing down into `models`) just calls `notify.NotifyXxx(...)`, and every registered listener reacts — without the caller knowing or importing any of them.

That's **dependency inversion**: instead of "low-level code imports high-level code" (backward, forbidden) or "one big function calls four services directly" (tight coupling), you define an interface at the point where the fan-out happens, and let each interested party plug itself in. You get the *effect* of bidirectional communication — an event flowing both to and from — without an actual bidirectional *dependency* in the import graph. It's the standard fix whenever you hit "but X really does need to react to Y" in a strictly layered system.

**Short version:** allowing real bidirectional deps has no upside that isn't better solved by an interface/callback at a layer boundary, and it costs you testability, comprehension, safe refactoring, and (in Go) the ability to build at all. Any case that looks like it needs two-way flow is usually a signal to introduce an interface, not to break the direction rule.
